Then he started Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. jumping all over him and when he got tired, he left and the man remained lying on the ground. After that, inmates took them into Dom and I never saw him but I heard that he survived.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You also described to the Court in the Stakic case the similarity between the accounts which were given by the inmates to whom you spoke as to how they had arrived at the camp, what had happened in their villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is Your Honours at page 7788 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't want you to repeat that evidence, doctor, because the Court is able to read it, but what you described was a pattern of happenings. From what you could see, was there any particular reason why a camp had been set up at Trnopolje? What was -- what was its advantages?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: You know, in the beginning, I never thought about it. I mean it never occurred to me. But later, after my last testimony, I started thinking about it because I was asked by the Defence, and they said that the camp had been set up there in haste. It was just an interplay of events but then I started thinking about it and I decided that it couldn't have been by accident, that somebody must have planned it well in advance, and that perhaps those who executed those particular order learned about it at the very last minute but if you look at the location of Trnopolje in that whole area, it is right next to the railway tracks and the railway station, and next to it a school with the cultural centre and the football field so that this is the ideal place in that area for a camp, a camp that would serve to round up the population there so that they could then be transported further on by truck or by rail. That was the ideal place, and it must have been done by somebody who was very familiar with that -- with the area, and who must have planned it well ahead. Why not in Kozarac? Why not somewhere else? Why in Trnopolje of all places?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've described, and you described in your previous testimony, the various convoys. Did -- before anybody was allowed on the convoys did they have to sign various documents?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The convoys that were organised regularly for women, children and the elderly, and at times a man would manage to join them here and there or perhaps a Serb friend would help him join them, I do not know that any documents were signed then. But the last transport, that is the convoy that was organised by the International Red Cross and the UNHCR, with which we, the registered inmates left, then the condition for us to leave was to sign a document leaving all our property to the Serb -- to Srpska Republika, or the autonomous region, I can't remember exactly, and one of the conditions was for the International Red Cross and the UNHCR to guarantee that we would never return to Bosnia, that we would be displaced and go to third countries rather than ever come back. The International Red Cross told us that we could sign it because it would have no force because it had been done under duress and so that some benches were put in front of the school and as the inmates were passing one by one to enter the buses, they first had to sign such sheets of paper. Unfortunately, everybody was given a copy of that, but I just tore up mine and threw it away but I'm sure that one of the inmates who left on that occasion is still in possession of this sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, have you ever been back to Prijedor since you were expelled?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I've never been to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us earlier you left on one of the last convoys in September, 1992. I think you were taken to Karlovac. On the same bus that you were, were there also the survivors of the - as it's called - the Mount Vlasic massacre?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Only after the people from the convoy had entered the buses is when I learnt that there were also six individuals with us whom the International Red Cross - I don't know how - succeeded in getting out from the hospital in Banja Luka, and smuggled them through. So as to help them to get out, together with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, this, doctor, I think you were asked by the Presiding Judge, Judge Schomburg, on the last occasion, whom you held responsible for what happened, and you gave a long answer which I'm not going to ask you to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours will find that at page 7863, onwards. Yes, thank you very much, doctor. Can you just wait there, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman. You're now going to be cross-examined by the Defence lead counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, doctor.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've probably noticed in some of the remarks you've heard here today that we are hoping we can finish with your testimony this morning, and you can aid us in that and yourself, I suppose, if you would try very hard to answer the questions that I ask you as concisely and quickly as you possibly can. If I need you to elaborate on an answer, I'll let you know that. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you gave in addition to the testimony in Stakic, you also gave a statement to the Prosecutor, and I'm going to refer to some of the things you said in that statement. Please understand that there -- if there is a time when you are not certain that my account of what you said in that statement is correct, you may have a copy of the statement and look at it and we'll get the Prosecutor to give you one and give you an opportunity to check it, okay?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On page 1 of that statement you gave to the Prosecutor, you talked about the situation prior to the war in 1992, and your words, according to that statement were, "Prior to the war, there were no problems between the ethnicities and we all got along fine." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Whether those were my exact words, I don't know but that is how it was and I can confirm it. Before the war, which broke out in the former Yugoslavia, not before the war in Prijedor but before the war, there were no problems, or at least I never noticed any because I never ran into any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You are aware of what happened in the general Prijedor-Kozarac area during World War II, are you not?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Up to a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know or did you know a person by the name of Hamdija Kahrimanovic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Kahrimanovic is a last name which I've heard, but Hamdija, whether I knew him, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He's a school teacher in Kozarac. Does that help you?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you agree with this statement. "Some of the most famous battles and some of the more horrible massacres of the war," referring to World War II, "were carried out in the shadows of the rugged Kozara mountains and residents were proud of their reputation as fierce fighters." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That is what books say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is a local saying from Kozarac, and I'll quote it for you. "People of Kozara love their guns like a girl. They love song and their glass of brandy but most of all they love their freedom." Are you familiar with that saying?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, but people from Kozara are not Serbs only. There are other ethnic groups, apart from Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm talking about all the people from Kozara, I think, when you talk about that saying, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I do think that there is such a saying, whether it is correct and to what degree, I cannot say. Everybody loves his freedom, not only people from Kozara. People in the Netherlands love their freedom too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes but the people in Kozara love their guns too, don't they?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I think there were many hunters who had hunting weapons, but of course, it varied from one individual to another. I had no affinity for weapons, nor did I ever own a weapon but I know a number of people from Kozara who never had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you agree that World War II bitterly divided the different groups in the region?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time, World War II, I was not taking part in it. How was it after the war, I was born in Kresevo near Sarajevo, and I only arrived in Kozarac after I'd graduated and did my military service so that I can't now tell you about the situation after World War II, and tell you either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you were taught history in elementary school and in every elementary school part of the history is what happened in the area of Mount Kozara and the slaughter of Serbs there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There was history and there were also men of advanced age who also told stories that were somewhat different from those that one found in books.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long it was after World War II that the situation changed, that these -- situation changed so that there were no problems between the ethnicities and you all got along fine, as you told us about? How long did it take for that to change?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: After the war, there must have been problems for a long time, I think Muslims did not have the right to say they were Muslims. They -- people could say they were Serbs or Croats but not as Muslims. That was permitted only later. I was born in 1959. And my childhood, the childhood that I remember, and throughout my life, I never had any problems with other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the constitution of 1974 that made it possible for Muslims to declare themselves Muslims?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I really can't tell you whether it was that constitution, but it was later on, yes, there was a constitution allowing Muslims to declare themselves as Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the Stakic case, at page 7719, you were asked about the effect -- I better tell you where I'm -- what I'm talking about. I'm talking about that period of time in 1991 when the war broke out in Croatia and there was a mobilisation of people. You said in the Stakic case at 7719, you were asked the effect that that mobilisation had on Serb attitudes toward the Muslim and Croat population in Prijedor. You answered that Muslims and Croats who failed to report for the mobilisation were tracked down by the military police and forcibly taken to the front. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you also told the Trial Chamber there that as a result of that, many Muslims and Croats went into hiding to avoid being tracked down and forcibly taken to the front. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And of course, if they were in hiding, they didn't go to work, did they?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if they didn't go to work, then they were likely dismissed from their jobs, correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't think that was the reason. In principle, one knew that dismissals from work started only when the military, and I think it was later February, took Prijedor and SDS by force. Before that, there were elections and the SDA had won in Prijedor, and there were Muslims still in responsible offices, together with Serbs and Croats, and the persecution had still not reached that level. That is the police was not yet persecuting people around the city openly. It was only after the army took Prijedor and when the SDS took over the power that all those -- all the Muslims and Croats who used to hold responsible positions were fired and those who had failed to sign loyalty and respond to mobilisation too. So I'm talking about early 1992 or possibly end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But wasn't it the law that if you didn't show up to work for a certain number of days, you were automatically dismissed from your job? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The majority of organisations could do that, but in the Prijedor case, where the SDA had won in the elections, the authority, the government, was not split yet, so that the attitude was more lenient. Rather before the army took it, people were not dismissed. It was only after that that they started being dismissed. Now, only. Now there is this period before and after. I know that after that, people began to be arrested, the curfew was introduced from as of 2100, and those who were arrested were taken to Mali Logor to the small camp in Banja Luka, and then were sent either to dig trenches on the front, some were exchanged, as prisoners of war, and some were forcibly mobilised and given weapons. Some of them returned in coffins with bullets in their backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you are I guess saying that once the SDA took power in Prijedor, that it was permitted for non-Serbs to stay away from their jobs and nothing would happen to them. They just didn't have to work. They would get paid but no work?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. It's not -- it is not correct. When the Serbs took over power in Prijedor, those who were in responsible positions, judges, or in the police, the chiefs there, all the non-Serbs were dismissed, and others...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it was translated improperly to you. The question I asked you was when the SDA, not the SDS, when the SDA was in charge in Prijedor, when they won the elections and took power, is it your position that during that period of time, non-Serb employees were permitted to not go to work and get paid and suffer no consequences from failing to show up for work?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you know about the situation in Prijedor at that time. The SDA, when it won, never succeeded in taking over, in assuming the authority, because the SDS blocked it. There were people who, if one learned that the military police was after somebody, then such people would not go to work. Perhaps, but it did not mean that people were absent from work for days on end because the military police wasn't there day in, day out, to see who would turn up for work and who wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told the Court in the Stakic case that it was the army that took over Prijedor, correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The troops took Prijedor physically, I think it was at nighttime that a military unit came from the front. I do not know which one. And it set up checkpoints around Prijedor to control those passing through, which placed snipers on buildings, took all the important institutions, the police building, the municipal hall, the hospital. There were police checkpoints in all those buildings and nobody could pass through without showing their IDs and immediately after, that the SDS took over the political authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Doctor, considering what we talked about at the beginning, about what would be fair, the question I asked you was: You told the Court in the Stakic case that it was the army that took over Prijedor. Couldn't that have just been answered yes, instead of that long, involved answer that you just gave?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I could have answered yes, yes -- no. Because you asked how the army took Prijedor, in different ways, the army did it physically and the SDS did it politically because the SDA had won the elections and it was when Bosnia was proclaimed a sovereign state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it's your position that it was the army that was rounding up people and taking them places like Keraterm and Omarska and Trnopolje, correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct, when we arrived in Trnopolje, there were very many soldiers and guards supervising it all, and all the checkpoints through which we went were manned by uniformed individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know who Sead Cirkin?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I've heard about Sead Cirkin. He's an active military. As far as I know, earlier, when the Serbs took Prijedor militarily, he tried to organise a defence of Kozarac in Kozarac. I do not know where he got it but he managed to put together some weapons and some guys who tried to organised Kozarac defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he headed a TO unit, an armed TO unit, in the Kozarac area, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was the Territorial Defence or what was it. What I heard was by and large that he tried to organise the defence of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware of a meeting prior to the occurrences in Kozarac, the fighting there, are you aware of a meeting where the question that was asked of the Kozarac people was whether they wanted to surrender their arms and avoid a conflict or not? Are you aware of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I only heard of a meeting, and that those in Kozarac were issued an ultimatum to lay down their weapons, but what exactly happened at the meeting, I don't know, because I was not present there, but I did hear about some negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware that those residents of Kozarac who attended that meeting, the persons who were proud of their reputation as fierce fighters and love their guns, resolved not to surrender their arms and to try to defend their village?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct, as far as I know they decided to defend their families and their village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you not aware that the actual fighting started in Kozarac when Muslims from a checkpoint there fired on a convoy of Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. I am not aware of that. As far as I know, the Serbs had already attacked on the other side, towards Ljubija, they had already attacked Hambarine and another locality and then moved from one village to the other. Kozarac was not the first place that was attacked by the Serb troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware that what happened at Hambarine was when Muslims fired at some Serb soldiers and killed a couple of them at Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Do you know that before that, Serb soldiers stopped a tractor carrying hay? They IDed the persons there. When they saw that they were Muslims, they killed them on the spot. We can chase each other with such examples for as long as you like but that won't lead to anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I tend to agree with you about that, sir. In the transcript at page 7722, you talked in the Stakic case about a meeting in Kozarac regarding a demand to put up Serb insignia and Serb flags and that an ultimatum was given to the people. Is that the same meeting that we were talking about just a moment ago? Or is that a different meeting?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many meetings there were, whether it was that one or whether there were several. The only thing I know is that I heard that the police and those who were organising were supposed to surrender, to declare their loyalty to the Serbs and to show or put up their insignia. This is what I heard. But I don't know whether you know that the police who surrendered during the surrender, each one of them was taken away and killed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were asked about checkpoints in the Kozarac area in the Stakic case, at page 7732 you told the Judges that you didn't notice, as far as the Muslim side is concerned, any checkpoints or weapons. When you would travel from Prijedor to Kozarac for your work, didn't you see the Muslim checkpoint near the crossroads, Prijedor-Banja Luka road Kozarac? Didn't you have to pass through it to get into Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: At the previous trial, I added something, on the main road, the Prijedor-Kozarac-Bana Luka road, I never saw any checkpoints on the Bosniak side but I remembered, when a tank was placed down there at the entrance to the Kozarac, then at the entrance to the sawmill, people from Kozarac set up barriers. There was also a guard there, in order to prevent the army and the tank from entering Kozarac but the others could pass through freely. Whether -- like I was asked whether there were any checkpoints at other places, outside of this road, perhaps at Kozarusa I don't know but I did hear that when the Serb army took over Prijedor and when they were indicating that they were going to take the Muslim settlements by force, then non-Serbs, Muslim and Croats, organised themselves and put up guards in order to defend themselves, in order to prevent the Serbs from entering the villages suddenly and committing a massacre. But this was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the witness's last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interpreter, sir, did not catch your last sentence. And I'll read out to you what we have. "I don't know but I did hear that when the Serb army took over Prijedor, and when they were indicating that they were going to take the Muslim settlements by force, then non-Serbs, Muslims and Croats, organised themselves and put up guards in order to defend themselves, in order to prevent the Serbs from entering the villages suddenly and committing a massacre. But this was" and this is where the interpreters did not catch up with you or understand what you said. What did you actually say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that this was only a reaction to the moves by the Serbs, who took over Prijedor militarily by force. Then the Muslims, fearing repercussions and for the safety of their families, organised some guards, which were supposed to prevent the Serbs from entering suddenly those parts inhabited by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman, sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, there was -- you've told us in the Stakic case and the Trial Chamber here also about the actual fighting that went on in Kozarac, the shooting that went on in Kozarac. You said that went on for a couple of days. And then after two days of shooting, which you heard from the basement of the medical centre, terms of surrender were agreed upon, correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm sorry, the word he used was "shelling."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is partially true. We were not at the clinic in the basement in Kozarac the whole time. When the surrender took place, we were at the relocated clinic on the outskirts of Kozarac, and then, at that point, the police managed to -- this was on the 26th -- to agree on the terms of surrender, and for the shelling to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Surrender, implies, doesn't it sir, that there was a battle going on, one side lost the battle and was surrendering their soldiers and their weapons, correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I wasn't present when this agreement was being reached, and I don't know what the terms were, but in any case, it was agreed that the police officers and the wounded, as well as the civilian population, should leave Prijedor. What their agreement was, and what happened, I don't know. I never heard of Cirkin afterwards. I don't know what happened to him. I just have to say that when the attack and the fighting were taking place, at that point, Cirkin and his men were not in Kozarac. They were probably outside of Kozarac somewhere, in some positions. In Kozarac, except for some members of the police, there weren't many armed men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I take it that it would not have taken two days for army, armed with artillery and tanks, to subdue a small village composed of nothing but unarmed and frightened civilians, would it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I've already told you that Cirkin had armed men who tried together with other civilians, these armed men had uniforms as well, I don't know if they were uniforms of the Territorial Defence or something else, but in any case, there was a type of armed formation that Cirkin had. I don't know what type or what kind it was. One time, I went to see Cirkin and there were some men with him and I assumed that others were up at their positions. The shelling, with small breaks, lasted until the -- lasted from the 24th, in the afternoon, and then it stopped at some point on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After this surrender that you talked about, the army effectively evacuated everyone from Kozarac, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. It was agreed that the civilians, the police officers and the wounded should leave Kozarac by themselves. The police was waiting outside, when everybody came out and surrendered, only at that point did the soldiers enter Kozarac. The only thing is that a lot of the -- many of the population were not aware, they didn't know about this surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And the first people who actually were lined up and allowed to leave Kozarac were the wounded people, correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I think it was the wounded, the wounded and the police but I think it was the wounded who went first. They were driven by the husband of Azra. He was driving the vehicle with the seriously wounded. I also need to tell you that in the meantime, a lot of them died. The young boy was still alive. He was allowed to pass through to Prijedor. A Muslim who had a bullet wound in the front was not allowed to go to the hospital. He was taken to Omarska. Also the driver who was driving the wounded was also sent immediately to Omarska. Only the Serb wounded person and the child were allowed to go to Prijedor. And the child died. And as far as the members of the police are concerned, I heard that they were killed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I now want to go to Trnopolje and ask you just a few questions about the food situation there. The Judges have had an opportunity to read your testimony in the Stakic case so we'll skip over a great deal of that. Food was brought into Trnopolje by local residents, people living around that area, including Serbs, correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's correct, in the beginning the Serbs were bringing food as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You -- you said in your statement, on page 8 of your statement to the Prosecutor, I'm quoting you, sir, "We couldn't leave outside of the barbed wire area unless a guard escorted us." The first thing I want to ask you about that, there was not barbed wire surrounding the entire camp, was there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that people who were staying there at Trnopolje were going out every day to work at their places of employment and coming back there to stay at night because it was a safe place?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That is not true. I am hearing this for the first time. That is not true at all, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Weren't lists kept of people who were permitted to go out and work during the day and where they worked, and all of those kinds of things? Weren't those lists kept there at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There were no such lists. I don't know about such lists. I'm sure that they did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it true that money was collected from people who were staying there at Trnopolje, collections taken up, so that bread and other food items could be purchased and brought into Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: At one point during the existence of the camp, money was collected from the inmates. We handed that money over to the Serbian Red Cross, and the next day, they would bring bread for the inmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And some of the people who made contributions had money because they were earning money at these outside jobs they were going to every day. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That is not true. I'm certain that that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that arrangements were made through and by the Serbian Red Cross to supply milk to the Trnopolje area on a daily basis for the children there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It's not true that it was a daily occurrence. We managed on our own initiative to agree or to make them agree to provide milk for the small children.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that people were permitted to go to their houses and gather up things like food items such as flour, sugar, whatever kind of food items they might have, and bring them to the camp? Beans and things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: During one period of the camp's existence, when there was no other choice, they did make it possible, under escort of soldiers, to go to nearby gardens and to pick beans and things. But it wasn't true that people went back to their own gardens and homes. They went to the nearby homes and gardens to bring back food. You could dig up potatoes, you could find tomatoes. It was already summer. So they allowed for a certain period, and this was after Penny Marshall came and until the arrival of the Red Cross, they allowed people to bring their own food in order to feed themselves. But it wasn't the people who were from those houses. And it was something that was carried out under guard escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The reason for the guard escort was to protect these people from roving bands of paramilitary criminals, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That was not so. The reason was so that the inmates wouldn't escape, even though I think that there was no sense in escaping because there were checkpoints all around, not only near the Trnopolje camp but also in that whole area. The reason why the guards went was to prevent the inmates from escaping.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: People were permitted to go to their homes and get wood stoves and firewood that they brought to Trnopolje for cooking purposes, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I am repeating once again that it wasn't people who were generally going to their own homes. It was inmates who happened to be there at the time, since the food had to be prepared somewhere, they allowed for furnaces to be brought, for wood to be brought, for this to be set up between the Dom and the school most frequently, and that that's where they were permitted to cook food for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 9 of your statement, "I never saw any politicians come to Trnopolje and I do not know any one in the Crisis Staff in Banja Luka." That's a true statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I didn't know anyone personally, and I said that I, in any case, don't know. Nobody at my clinic ever came and said, "I'm such and such a politician." There were some delegations that came to visit but who made up those delegations, I don't know. They weren't people that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, since you've raised it, what you said was that there was a delegation that came with an American and a high-ranking JNA officer. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There was a foreigner. I don't know whether it was an American or not. I don't know. I assume that it was. And there were several officers, one of whom was of a very high rank. I don't remember which rank. But there were several uniformed persons, Serbs, who they were I'm not -- I don't know. We talked. As they were going from one room to the next, the person who was interpreting for this gentleman, I managed to give her a sign, indicating that I wished to speak to them alone. She told that, whispered this into that gentleman's ear and he asked these people to leave the room, and then we talked alone, only with this politician, I don't know who it was, but this politician who was in civilian clothes, and who was a foreigner. There were other delegations as well that came, who did not even come into the clinic, but I don't know what these delegations were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You had said that this person, one of these people, was a very high-ranking JNA officer. Let me ask you if you know it was a JNA officer or was it a VRS officer?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to me what VRS is?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the difference is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So when you said it was a JNA officer, you just were referring to a high-ranking military person in a uniform that appeared to you to be JNA?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's correct. In any case, he was a member of the Serb side. I don't know if they had any special units or anything like that at that time. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On page 7748 of the Stakic transcript, you told the Judges that when you first arrived at Trnopolje, there was no outward indication that any kind of camp was being or had been established there. That's true, correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I said that I did not even think about a camp. It never even occurred to me. I saw a lot of soldiers, women and children. I wasn't expecting at all, I wasn't even thinking about any kind of camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was no wire or fencing that had not been there before, was there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There was a wire fence from before. There was a small wire fence around the school. And a higher fence around the shop that was selling construction material. And they existed from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Some of that fence was so low that you could actually jump over it, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. This low fence in front of the clinic could be jumped over without a problem, and even the fence that was around the school could easily be jumped over also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like to you look at Exhibit P1128.1, please. I think it might be 1128.12. Let's get -- I want the one with the red markings on it. It may be that the only copy is with the Prosecutor right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour for the purpose of the transcript, I think it's 1128.5. It's the last of the four plans. No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1128 are photos, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whatever it is, you mean the plan, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what I'm looking for is the plan that has the red fence drawn on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, that red line you've drawn on there, represents a fence that was constructed upon the arrival of men from Keraterm and Omarska, correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Shortly before they arrived, the fence was prepared for them, and then when they came, they were placed within the area that was encircled with the fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The south side of that fence that encloses the building materials store was already there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: This part that was in the south was already in place. That is the high fence around the construction-material shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was a barbed wire fence, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The barbed wire was at the top of the fence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the balance of that fence that was installed right before the Keraterm-Omarska people came was not a barbed wire fence but a chain-link fence, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. I think that on this side, there was a wire mesh, mesh, and it wasn't very high, maybe 1.5 metres at the most on this side towards the road and towards the Dom, the fence was about a man's height high. And at the top it did have one row of barbed wire. That's this side next to the road, towards the hole -- the Dom. This side of the fence was a little lower and it did not have any barbed wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know whether you know this or not and if you don't, you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. can just tell me. But it's the case, isn't it, that when Penny Marshall came the first time and photographed people at Trnopolje, she went inside that barbed wire fence where the construction building is and filmed through the fence from inside that area so as to show the barbed wire on that side of the fence. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: She was photographing people and on those photographs, you can see people from this side. So from this area here, which is around the hardware shop fenced, from this fenced area, she was also taking photographs of people who were on the other side of the wire within fenced in -- within a different type of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, this fence, this red line that you've drawn there, only stayed there for about, at a maximum, I think you said, two weeks, and then it was taken down, correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. That wire wasn't there long, when the first people arrived from Keraterm and Omarska, they were put here. Immediately after that, Penny Marshall arrived and after that, a large group from Omarska also arrived and they were put here in this area, fenced -- that is within the fence around the hardware store, and after that, this fence here was removed and the door was opened here. So that that was -- that it was taken away after a short time. It wasn't there long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, whenever it's convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me just ask one or two more questions about this and then we can break, would that be okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So during that ten days that that fence was there, none of the other inmates, none of the other people that were there at Trnopolje, were confined within that fence, it was just the Keraterm and Omarska people, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: At that time, it was only those inmates who were brought and put within that fence so Keraterm and part of Omarska, in this other fenced-off part. Later on, when this was removed, after the journalists, the inmates were allowed to mingle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. This is a good time for the break. I wonder if we can make it 15 minutes so we can try to finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will just have a short break of 15 minutes and then we will try to make every effort to finish with the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, in your testimony in Stakic, at page 7787, you said the men were not allowed to leave the camp. Actually, unless they were kept inside that ten day fence we talked about, at night they could simply go over that fence and leave, couldn't they? In various parts of the camp, they could just go through the fence, over the fence, and walk away if they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Well, it was possible, like in any other prison. One could organise escape. So I suppose one could organise escape from the Trnopolje camp. If you look at how the guards were deployed, you will then see that it wouldn't have been all that easy. That is one thing. Secondly, the question arises, once you've escaped from the camp, where do you go then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was my next question. What would be the motive for someone to leave there? Where would they go?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Well, the Serbs controlled more or less everything. So you could only hide in the forest somewhere, on Kozara or try to cross the mountains and reach Croatia or the free territory. So that if somebody was certain that Serbs will find him on some list or killed perhaps would opt for that but the majority of civilians like myself thought that after all, we were civilians, we were not taking part in the war. We were not concerned with it basically and we expected that -- and we didn't expect that somebody would kill us just because we were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know anybody who did what you suggested, left the camp and went through the mountains and made their way to safety?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. I do not know. I don't know. And the name of a single individual who, for instance, left Trnopolje and did that. I know that some groups from Kozarac tried to go through the mountains and reach Croatia but I do not know if anyone from Trnopolje did that. I do not have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Sejmenovic first name Mevludin?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Sejmenovic Mevludin? Yes, it rings a bell. I think he was in the SDA. I think he was politically active.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that he entered Trnopolje on his own at night, stayed there for a period of time, left Trnopolje, was gone for a period of time, and then returned to Trnopolje again? Do you know that that happened?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. As far as I know, he was taken to Omarska. How he entered the Trnopolje camp, I do not know. Perhaps one could, when food was collected, if the guard was inattentive then perhaps somebody could sneak into the camp. One cannot exclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that people did not want to leave the Trnopolje area because that was the safest place in the area?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That is not true. It depends to what period of time do you have in mind. Towards the end, when the International Red Cross arrived, as of that time, when the inmates were registered, as of that time it would be true that it was safer in the camp, when the International Red Cross had registered the inmates and carried out regular controls, than outside in one's own house because Serbs came -- went regularly there, and harassed and took people away so as of the moment when the International Red Cross arrived and registered people, then it was better to be in a way in a camp than outside it but not until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said initially that at Trnopolje there were no beds, no cots, no blankets and that everyone just had to sleep on the floor or on the ground, correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: In Trnopolje, only what was there when people arrived, so there are no beds in schools, a school has desks. In the clinic, there were those two beds. Of course people somehow made do. Some of those who came to Trnopolje managed to come by a blanket, even people who lived around Trnopolje provided us with two or three blankets even but it was all on an individual basis. It depended on how one knew how to manage. Some knew guards and there were also guards who tried as far as they could to help us. I did not say that all Serbs are the same, and that there were not -- that there were not Serbs who were against what was happening or who would refuse to help us. There were Serbs who wanted to help us and did help us as much as they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it your sense that there were a lot of beds and blankets there in Trnopolje that could have been provided for the people that were there and were just withheld out of meanness or something like that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. In Trnopolje, there were only private houses, which means that apart from those beds from private houses, there were simply no other beds. Whether they could have been brought from somewhere else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that many, many people who were at Trnopolje came there voluntarily, on their own, because it was a safe place and because it was a place where they might be able to get --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have asked him this question already, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know but there is a different kind of question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Because it was a safe place and because there was an opportunity to find a convoy to leave the area? Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of that being the case. As far as I know, after the cleansing of the village, people would be brought to the camp in order to organise convoys. I know that there were some exceptions, that every individual who, through some of their Serb friends, would come on the eve of the convoys so as to join it and leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, at one point you gave some kind of a statement. It's called an interview with Dr. Idriz Merdzanic, interviewed in Karlovac. Do you remember being interviewed there and a statement taken from you?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Possibly. I think it was somebody from the U.S. Embassy who came and took statements from inmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is a statement that was attached to your statement that was given me by the Office of the Prosecutor, and I don't know quite how to refer to. It has an ERN number of 00288977. And at the bottom it says, "Page 34." And according to this, it says that you said, with regard to Trnopolje, "People were coming in from all over. Sleeping in their cars and farm machinery, up to 9.000 or 10.000." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Perhaps when you read it within this context, it turns up that people came, but people were being evicted from their houses and taken under custody to Trnopolje. So of course you get there, if somebody forces you out of a house, and then brings you there under custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talked about your clinic at Trnopolje being very short of medicines of various kinds. One of the things were you able to do, wasn't it, was to go out to the surrounding houses, the houses in the area, and find medicines and bring them back to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It depended on who was on guard duty. Often, there would be some Serb guards who lived in Trnopolje or somewhere nearby. I knew those lads, and with some of them, I could talk and ask them to escort me so as a rule, myself and Azra and I believe his name was Nisevic, a soldier who stood guard, and who was always ready to help us. So he allowed it, and organised it for us, to visit other houses and try to find some medicines but it depended on the guards and not every guard shift would allow us to do it, only some that we knew well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would it be accurate to describe Trnopolje as a transit camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Trnopolje is undoubtedly for a major part, perhaps even the chief purpose of Trnopolje, was in point of fact the deportation of the Muslim population from the area, whereas the men's part was something else but it was like two camps in one, one where people were brought, transport, gathered, transported and then banished from the Serb area. Those were the women, children, and the elderly and possibly some men too who managed to join them and those others who were of military age, they were not allowed to leave, presumably because they were able-bodied men or -- and for some reasons, in Trnopolje were mostly people in whom Serbs were not interested. All those in whom they were interested, they took to Omarska or Keraterm. So that Trnopolje was perhaps the best of all these camps. Except that amongst those people who were Trnopolje, they would search for some of those they were interested in. But I think that the chief purpose of that camp was forcible transfer of the Muslim population, because if one looks at the system that they used, first to have Serb armed forces, which would clean, sweep up the village, then they would come to Trnopolje, then taken over by the Serb Red Cross, they organised the transfers, allegedly they are helping with those convoys, they are helping people to transfer, and then some charitable Serb organisation or something like that, turn up, and they settle in Muslim and Croat homes Serbs from other areas. I think this was developed down to the minutest detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is no way we are going to finish today if you don't answer my questions. The question I asked you was simple: Would it be accurate to describe Trnopolje as a transit camp. It would be easy to answer "yes" or "no". We are going to be here to tomorrow if you can't just answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman is right. You're not answering the questions. You're telling us things that we -- you aren't being asked to tell.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I apologise, for the Trnopolje camp could be described also as a camp for the deportation of the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you, and I'm referring now to that period of time at Trnopolje before the arrival of the Red Cross and the registration of the people there, there were plenty of soldiers around with guns at that point in time, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: You mean before the International Red Cross came?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There were guards, say, in the earliest days, there were very many military people there, a few days later organised guards were set up and Major Kuruzovic arrived and there were guards around the clock in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There were machine-guns in the machine-gun nests that you described, right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I've already described it and said that it depended on the guards who took up duty. Every shift brought their own weapons and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not the answer that you have been asked to give. The question was: "There were machine-guns in the machine-gun nests that you described, right?" Answer yes or no. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've described in your testimony in Stakic how a few people, including the Foric people, for instance, were actually shot and killed, correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I was not present at the killing but I believe they were shot dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There were certainly plenty of weapons and plenty of soldiers to have shot and killed everybody in Trnopolje, weren't there? They could have done that.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. They could have killed everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They could have killed all the men from Keraterm instead of bringing them to Trnopolje, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the same true of the men who were brought from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the materials that were given us with regard -- and attached to your statement, there was a transcript from a case in England, the United Kingdom, that you testified in. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm just curious: What was that case about?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That case had to do with that wire. That was the chief subject, because the other side claimed that there has never been any camp there, that there has never been any wire there, and just as you are claiming now, that it wasn't a camp at all, that people could come and go at will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's where it came out actually, wasn't it, that Penny Marshall had gone inside that barbed wire enclosed compound so as to take pictures from inside there making it appear that the camp was surrounded by barbed wire? I mean that was part of the contention there, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour I'm sorry I object to the words used, came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I withdraw the question. I don't even want it answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At page 7789 of the Stakic transcript, you said this: "Even the arrival of the journalists only took place, as far as I know, after Karadzic had granted his approval." You may not know this but if you do, tell me, isn't it the case that Karadzic was confronted at the London conference with media reports regarding Omarska. He denied that such camps existed. On additional pressure, he then ordered authorities in the Prijedor area to allow access to these areas where it was claimed that camps existed? Isn't that the way it happened?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I do not know how things happened. All I heard was that Karadzic was the one who had authorised the visit to the camps by journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know that even with Karadzic authorising those visits, the authorities at Omarska would not permit the journalist to visit many parts of that camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That is something that I learned afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, as far as you know, the only convoy leaving Trnopolje that required people to sign these documents, relinquishing their property, was that one that was organised by the ICRC and the UNHCR, correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you were advised, or the people were advised, after questioning it, by the ICRC, that they should go ahead and sign them, quote, this is your testimony, sir, "Because no laws will acknowledge such documents and you can sign it without worrying because those documents would not be used." That's what you said in Stakic, correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Very briefly I want to ask you a question or two about the issue of rapes occurring at Trnopolje. You had indicated that at least to some extent those rapes were committed by a group of soldiers from a tank unit who called themselves El Maniacos. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know anything about that unit, do you know where they were from, who they were, anything about them at all?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, I know nothing about that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There came a time, didn't there, when the commander of Trnopolje, Major Kuruzovic I think was his name, actually had one of the soldiers accused of coming into the camp and raping women, had him arrested and had him in confinement, true?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know if Major Kuruzovic did that. What I heard was that one of those soldiers had been locked up in the barracks in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And at least somebody thought it their duty to try to punish this particular soldier for what he had done, correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this happened after the authorities at Trnopolje were persuaded to allow some of these women to be taken to Prijedor for examinations to determine if, in fact, they had been raped, correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct, but I talked with Dr. Dusko Ivic. He is also a physician. And I don't know who did he talk to. But whatever the case, he took some of those women to Prijedor for examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Dr. Dusko Ivic was a Serb doctor, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, when the rest of the soldiers from this tank group, El Maniacos learned that one of their members had been arrested and was confined at the barracks in Prijedor, they went there with their tanks, pointed the tanks at the barracks, and demanded his release, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: What I heard was that they set him free, but how, whether with tanks and pointing their guns, I don't know. But I heard that they got their member free.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, wasn't that your testimony? That it was tanks pointing at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there, so that I don't know whether they were aiming at the barracks or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During the Stakic testimony, it's actually a videotape that was played, and during that videotape, a narrator says, we may have seen it today "Dr. Idriz says that Trnopolje camp military commander once tried to discipline a rapist." And then apparently you say, "When the rest of the soldiers found out about that," I'm on page 7798, "When the rest of the soldiers found out about that, they got drunk and drove two tanks in front of the main military barracks and gave an ultimatum that the soldier had to be released or else they would shoot at their own barracks so they released the soldier." Now, there is a video, sir, of you saying that, apparently at one point it was your understanding that that's what had happened or were you just making that up?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No soldier was arrested at Trnopolje in any case, any rapist. I did hear that one of those soldiers were arrested -- was arrested and placed in the barracks, and then those tank operators freed him. They also later came to Trnopolje with two tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If they actually went to the barracks and pointed their tanks at the barracks and demanded the release of their fellow soldier, that certainly wasn't within what you would understand normal military discipline, was it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I heard the witness answer but I didn't get the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard him say,"tacan."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He said, "tacan."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your first statement to the Prosecutor, at page 17, you said this. I'm asking if you recall saying it, "Before the journalists came the Serbs dismantled Keraterm so it looked like no one was ever there. The same happened with Omarska." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It's possible that I said that, because they did dismantle Keraterm, and if you continue reading my statement, I think that I said that Omarska was partially disbanded and that a certain number of inmates stayed, for whom beds were prepared and food was made and then they were later shown to journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going there. You know that when the journalists first visited Omarska however there were a large number of people still confined there, those people later came to Trnopolje or some of them did. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know where they were, in any case, they hadn't arrived at Trnopolje yet. The journalists did not see them at Omarska and did not have access to all of the rooms. I don't know where those people were at that time, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like to you look at Exhibit P1134, please. Sir, what you have before you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Your Honours have seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you have before you is a document entitled "Report of the commission on the inspection of collection centres, other facilities for captives, in the Autonomous Region of Krajina," and it's dated Pale, 17 August, 1992. What I want to do is direct your attention to part II of that document, a section headed, "Omarska, near Prijedor." And you'll find a paragraph that begins with, "The prisoners are kept."

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says, "The prisoners are kept in a hall containing military camp beds and orderly toilet facilities. Food is provided for them in the workers' canteen. The food is prepared in the mine's central building and is provided on a self-service basis. First aid point is located in one of the offices and is staffed by a physician and a nurse to administer any first aid that may be required. While the more serious cases, the prisoners are transferred to the medical centres in Banja Luka and Prijedor." Now, you have previously said that you were aware that after most of the people were removed from Omarska, that the number of people that stayed there were given food and army beds and sheets so that when the journalists went there a second time, they saw a fairly regular situation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's true. I talked with many inmates from Omarska who had been there and what I know is that those beds were made up before the arrival of the journalists so as to show to the journalists conditions that did not actually prevail. There are many witnesses from Omarska. I wasn't at Omarska so I cannot testify about Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The statement that we just read from this report, is that not consistent with what you heard?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. It does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Turn back to the section labelled with a number 1, "Trnopolje, near Prijedor." Understanding that we are talking about August of 1992, in the second paragraph, "The number of residents at this centre changes daily because their movement is in no way restricted and they can leave for a destination of their own choice after obtaining the relevant documents." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: A part of that is true. After the journalists visited, when the wire was taken down, it was permitted for visits to take place at the camp, which means that women who had their husbands or children at the camp were permitted to come to the camp, even to bring food. They would leave their ID card with the guards and after a certain amount of time, they could leave again, take their ID card back, and leave the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I have just a very few more questions to ask you. I want to look at the photograph again, P1128-26, I believe is the one I want to see and have you look at. That's it. Now, sir, that's a photograph of the entry area to the clinic you described where the dentist's offices were and things of that nature, correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the clinic in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this is taken about four years after the fighting that went on there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Taken in 1996, correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there had been damage done to that building by vandalism in the intervening nearly four years, hadn't there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I think that there was also some damage that was caused by the weather, with the passage of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It appears that there has been a flood there. If you look at those polls that sit in front of that thing there, the black that comes way up to the top of the steps, that's indicative of there being a flood and that having all been under water, isn't it? Do you know anything about a flood occurring there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, Kozarac is elevated, especially the clinic, so it's not possible for that area to be flooded. In order for floods to come up that high, there would have to be a lot of rain. Everything would have to be soaked and the level of water to be high enough to come into the clinic building, I cannot believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. The -- this clinic was a clinic for the whole of the Kozarac area, was it not?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... treatment of everybody that lived there. It wasn't just a Muslim clinic, was it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's correct, and also the people who worked there were not only Muslims. Other people worked there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that symbol you see in two places on that building, the circle with the X in it, that had nothing to do with that being a Muslim building, did it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. I don't think that that had anything to do with that because that wouldn't make sense because it wasn't a Muslim building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That symbol, in fact -- maybe you don't know this, that symbol is an international symbol that I understand that deals with buildings that are dangerous, under repair, things of that nature, it tends to be a warning to stay out, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know that. I'm not familiar with such symbols.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In speaking during your direct examination about people getting on the convoys and leaving Trnopolje, you used the phrase, "People who were banished from the territory." Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it true that people were basically clamouring to get on those buses? They were demanding to get on those buses and get out of there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's correct. People wanted ultimately to leave that territory as fast as possible so that they would not be exposed to danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know, it was very early, very shortly after your arrival at Trnopolje, that the Serbian Red Cross arrived, correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know if the Serbian Red Cross was ever in Keraterm or Omarska?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Trnopolje, to the extent that it had administration, it was all army, wasn't it? The commander was military, the guards were military and so forth?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. Baltic Rade was there often as well as Ostoja Skrbic as civilians. Whether they had some part or role in that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The pictures that were taken with the camera that Azra had brought into Trnopolje of Nedzad Jakupovic, the two pictures that were you shown earlier, you said that when you took these pictures, you were trying to do it in a way so that the person whose picture was being taken would not be aware that he was being photographed. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: In any case, we hoped that that person would not notice that they were being photographed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It looks to me like these pictures were taken with a flash. Am I wrong about that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. Perhaps you're right. Yes, perhaps they were taken with a flash. Azra would know whether the camera had a flash. But I think that you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see the video where Nedzad Jakupovic describes how he -- how his eye was injured?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. It's possible that I did see it but I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did he tell you how his eye was injured?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Not particularly about his eye. He was beaten on several occasions. We only photographed that the first time. Later we also had more contacts with him and he told us that he was beaten, that he had received a beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did he tell you that he injured his eye when he was trying to leap out of a window and hit the wall instead?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. He didn't tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You spoke about the document that you were asked to sign before you were put on the last convoy and taken from Trnopolje. You said you tore yours up and threw it away. Does that mean you refused to sign it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. Only when I left the camp, when we arrived at Karlovac, I don't know whether this was out of rage or something, but I took it and I tore it up, and now I wish that I had kept it. I had to sign it, and I ripped it up only after I left Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You actually signed it and there should be a copy of it somewhere, the one you signed?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You asked by Ms. Korner if you have been back to Prijedor since you were, and this was her word, expelled. Tell us what you did to try to keep from going on that last convoy?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? I didn't do anything not to get into that convoy. I was registered and of course I wanted to be included in the convoy just like the other inmates, because I wanted to leave that territory, where there was a danger every day for somebody to come and kill you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The last thing that Ms. Korner asked you was about a question and she really didn't go into it very much but a question that was asked you by Judge -- one of the Judges, I think it was Judge Schomburg in Stakic. It was Judge Schomburg, with regard to who was responsible for what happened. And you gave a fairly long answer to that question that was primarily your guesses as to what -- who might have been responsible. But the fact is you have no idea, do you?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there any re-examination, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you have wanted to leave your home in Prijedor and your clinic if the attack on Kozarac had not taken place?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Of course I wouldn't want to leave that area, if the war and all of those events hadn't come about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you got on that bus and went and were taken to Karlovac, you told us that you wanted to get out, were you doing that voluntarily, of your free will?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. What do you mean? Did I want to get on the bus voluntarily or did I want to go further once I reached Karlovac? I'm not sure about the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you got on that bus, on one of the last buses that left Trnopolje, was that because you wanted to leave the Prijedor region for good?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I didn't think that I would be leaving that area for good but at that moment, I was happy to be leaving that place. I did think that I would come back one day, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were happy to be leaving that place why?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Because the uncertainty in the camp, that any day, anybody could come in and kill you or beat you up, was unbearable, not only for me but for the majority of those in the camp or who were staying in houses. They were all happy to leave that area so that they would no longer be in danger.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Merdzanic, that brings your testimony to an end. And you should be able to return home pretty quickly. As you see, your testimony lasted just this sitting and that's very good. However, before you leave this courtroom, it is my responsibility and my wish to thank you for having accepted to come again to this Tribunal to give evidence, and I can assure you that you will be taken care of between now and your return to your country. The usher will escort you out of the courtroom and you'll be attended to as necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And so that being it, we will resume on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we meet in the afternoon on the 20th, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is one matter I want to bring to your attention and maybe you can just pass a word to facilitate this. We had a near problem over being able to proceed today, and that was this: I provided Mr. Brdjanin with the tapes from Stakic of this witness's testimony. When he was taken from here to the detention centre they took them away from him. They said they would give it back to him that evening, they didn't. He called me Saturday morning to tell me he didn't have the tapes. I started making inquiry of the detention centre. They finally were able to locate them. They had given them to some other detainee, which in itself is cause for alarm because what if this had been Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a protected witness? And somehow, there has to be a mechanism worked out where I can give him these tapes and he can take them to his cell without them being given to people who probably have no business looking at them in the first place, especially if we are dealing with protected witnesses and fortunately I was able, with several phone calls on Saturday to emphasise how important it was and he was able to get them by noon on Saturday and then he and I were able to have a conversation late Sunday about his having listened to them. So fortunately it was a short witness and he was able to listen to them in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman, for bringing this up. The Chamber orders that this part of the transcript is copied and communicated to Mr. Tim McFadden for his information and any appropriate action that may be necessary now and in the future, particularly with a view to avoiding repetitions of this accident, of this incident. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only query I have is Your Honour was going to make an inquiry and from the point of view of organising witnesses as to whether we were going to find a court to sit on Friday, the 22nd, because at the moment we are in a court that has court maintenance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we really -- if Your Honours could or your legal staff could get us a message so we know which witnesses to organise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, please liaise with Madam Chuqing as she was supposed to have worked on this and what the situation would be. And as soon as there is a possibility of reply, of feedback, please let everyone know about it. Okay. Thank.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour I must know by tomorrow who the witness will be on the 20th or that it will be one of two or three witnesses because I have to get the tapes to Mr. Brdjanin on Tuesday. I can't get them to him after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour we can certainly let Mr. Ackerman know who is coming on the 20th. It's a question of who else is coming up that week because as I recall, all of the people listed are all effectively like today's witness, shortish. But that's why I say I agree with Mr. Ackerman if we could know tomorrow please whether we've got the Court then we can actually give the definitive list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you all. See you on the 20th. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1.45 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 20th day of November, 2002, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
